parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπαρχίᾱ (eparkhíā).
Phono-semantic matching of Ancient Greek αἰθήρ (aithḗr, “upper air”).
From Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous).

parole.significato: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see أُذْن (ʔuḏn), فَأْر (faʔr)
parole.testo: Literally “ear of the mouse”, calque of Ancient Greek μυοσωτίς (muosōtís, literally “mouse-ear”), probably via its calque Classical Syriac ܐܹܕܢܲܝ ܥܘ݂ܩܒܪ̈ܐ pl (ʾeḏnay ʿuqbǝrē, literally “mouse-ear”) which is also transmitted corruptly as an alleged **عَنْقَر (**ʕanqar), which should be corrected to ع
From Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀρτέμων (artémōn). Also found as Classical Syriac ܐܰܪܛܶܡܘܿܢܳܐ (arṭemōnā) and Latin artemōn.

parole.significato: one of the principal and fundamental elements or hypostases that keep together the material world or a personification…
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἄρχων (árkhōn, “ruler”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄσαρον (ásaron).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek στοιχάς (stoikhás).

parole.significato: myth, fable, tale, legend, story especially full of embellishments
parole.testo: From phono-semantic matching of Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía), with the native Arabic سَطَرَ (saṭara, “to write, to compose lines”).
From أسطورة, meaning 'legend', which is itself from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía).
An old borrowing of Ancient Greek στόλος (stólos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀσπάραγος (aspáragos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek στομαχικόν (stomakhikón).
أَطْلَس (ʔaṭlas, “Atlas”) + ـِيّ (-iyy), after the model of Ancient Greek ἀτλαντικός (atlantikós) and Latin atlanticus, from the name of the Titan Ἄτλας (Átlas) (genitive Ἄτλαντος (Átlantos)).

parole.significato: dodder (Cuscuta gen. et spp., especially Cuscuta epithymum)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐπίθυμον (epíthumon, “hellweed (Cuscuta epithymum)”)
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀψίνθιον (apsínthion). Doublet of إِسْفِنْط (ʔisfinṭ) borrowed earlier.
Via Middle Persian and directly from Ancient Greek ὄπιον (ópion).

parole.significato: various kinds of thistles mainly of the Cynareae and Cichorieae tribes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄκανθα (ákantha) and ἀκάνθιον (akánthion).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀναγαλλίς (anagallís).
From Ancient Greek ἄγκῡρα (ánkūra), possibly via Classical Persian لنگر (langar) with rebracketing. However, other Greek nautical terms reached Arabic directly.

parole.significato: (juice of grapes, oil of olives, etc) extracted unripe from the fruit
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὀμφάκιον (omphákion, “juice from unripe grapes; oil from unripe olives”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄνισον (ánison), ultimately from Egyptian jnst.
From Ancient Greek οὐροβόρος (ourobóros, “tail-devouring”, a compound of οὐρά (ourá, “tail”) + -βόρος (-bóros, “-devouring”, which is derived from the verb βιβρώσκω (bibrṓskō, “to eat up”))).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀορτή (aortḗ).

parole.significato: a kind of estate privileged from taxes
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek οὐσία (ousía).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ὠκεανός (Ōkeanós). Doublet of قَامُوس (qāmūs).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek εἰκών (eikṓn). Sense 2 is a semantic loan from English icon.

parole.significato: the sludge left behind by a river that has retreated, alluvium
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek πηλός (pēlós, “clay”), or ἰλύς (ilús, “mud, slime”) with the Coptic ⲡⲓ- (pi-) masculine singular definite article, though ἰλύς (ilús, “mud, slime”) is feminine and would require ϯ- (ti-); originally this word was applied particularly to the alluvial deposit of the Nile.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek σπόγγος (spóngos).

parole.significato: wedge (in many senses, including in wedge-writing and as a simple machine)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek σφήν (sphḗn, “wedge”), probably also through Classical Syriac ܐܣܦܢܐ (ʾespēnā), ܣܦܝܢܐ (sp̄īnā, “wedge”). However in the sense sphene, titanite its alternative form has, it is from French sphène from the same Greek word, for mineralogist René Just Haüy has coined this name in 1801 (

From Ancient Greek σκίλλα (skílla). Perhaps more often rendered by ش (š) in Arabic, otherwise rare in Greek borrowings save for historical laminal /s/ pronunciation in Vulgar Latin or Romance engendering it, because in Classical Syriac in which the word had spread earlier it had ܣ (s) which correspo

parole.significato: region, climate (geographical area of the earth, particularly a zone of latitude)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κᾰδμείᾱ (kădmeíā).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek κνίδιον (knídion), from Κνίδος (Knídos). First attested in the Ptolemaic period and the most widely attested amphora name in Late Antiquity in Greek and also popular in Coptic (ⲕⲛⲓⲕⲓϫⲓ (knikiji), ⲕⲛⲓⲕⲓⲇⲓ (knikidi), ⲕⲟⲩⲛⲇⲟⲩ (koundou), as an equivalent of ⲗⲁⲕⲟⲟⲧⲉ (lakoote))
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix), allegedly via Classical Syriac.

parole.significato: bilge, sink of a ship, well room
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἀγκύλη (ankúlē, literally “bend”).
From إِنِّي (ʔinnī, “Indeed, I am”), composed of إِنَّ (ʔinna, an emphasizing sentence particle) + ـنِي (-nī, “me”). Also often hypothesized to be from Ancient Greek εἶναι (eînai, “be, exist”).

parole.significato: hiera picra, a kind of cathartic, laxative, and allround treacle of complicated composition
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek ἱερᾱ́ πίκρα (hierā́ píkra, literally “divine bitter”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek βάτος (bátos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Πάνθειον (Pántheion, “a temple of all gods”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πέταλος (pétalos).

Probably one of the words Yemenite expatriates picked up in the Byzantine Empire, from Ancient Greek πυρός (purós), similar to فِرْسِك (firsik, “peach”), if it is correct that one has to posit for Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥ a meaning “spelt”. Another word for spelt or dinkel wheat is borrowed from
Borrowed from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros).
From بَرْبَر (barbar, “Berbers”) + ـِيّ (-iyy), probably from Ancient Greek βάρβαρος (bárbaros, “non-Greek, foreign, barbarian”), apparently imitative of foreign speech.
Etymology 1, noun sense 3, Etymology 1, noun sense 4 are calques of Ancient Greek εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”). Compare Hebrew בְּשׂוֹרָה (bəśorá, “good tidings, good news, gospel”).

Causative of بَشِرَ (bašira, “to rejoice at”). Religious sense is a literal translation of Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō), from εὐαγγέλιον (euangélion, “good news, gospel”). Cognate with Hebrew בִּשֵׂר (bisér, biśśēr, “to bring good news”).
Probably from Ancient Greek πιττάκιον (pittákion).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek πῠ́ξος (pŭ́xos).
From Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “phlegm, a cold slimy humour of the body”).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἱππιατρός (hippiatrós), from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + ἰατρός (iatrós, “physician”). Cognate with Aramaic אִפִּיטְרוּס (ʾippīṭrūs), Classical Syriac ܦܝܛܪܐ (pyaṭrā) and ܒܛܪܐ (baṭrā). Reinterpreted as from the root ب ط ر (b ṭ r) related to “slashing, cutting”, because the f
From Ancient Greek θυρεός (thureós), ultimately the same source as etymology 2.
Ancient Greek θαιρός (thairós, “a pivot of a door or gate; mechanism to open a door”), from Ancient Greek θῠ́ρᾱ (thŭ́rā, “door, entrance”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰwer-.

From Ancient Greek τίμημα (tímēma), from τιμή (timḗ), from τῑ́ω (tī́ō), leveled to the root ث م ن (ṯ m n); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷey- (“value, honor”). Compare Classical Syriac ܛܝܼܡܵܐ (ṭīmā, “price, value”) and Jewish Literary Aramaic תמא (tmˀ, “duty, tax, fee”); for more see τιμή (t
ثِيُوقْراط (ṯiyūqrāṭ, “theocrat”) + ـِيّ (-iyy); derived from Ancient Greek θεοκρατία (theokratía), from θεος (theos, “god”, “deity”) + -κρατία (-kratía, “power, rule”).

Late borrowing from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos), likely via an Aramaic form exposing an arbitrary extension of Late Koine Greek style or origin as reflected in Classical Syriac ܓܘܦܣܝܢ (gupsīn), ܓܝܦܣܝܢ (gipsīn) and Jewish Palestinian Aramaic גבסין, גפסין. It is unknown whether the Greek term is ulti
From Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

From Ancient Greek χαλκός (khalkós, “copper”). The cosmetic and the art of its application are vulgarly claimed to be of Punic substrate. The word has probably been borrowed on two occasions regardless of it, the ر (r) form being a previous popular borrowing, wherefor the pigment and dipterans meani

Partial calque of translingual Artocarpus (literally “bread-fruit”); as the feminine inflection of Arabic خُبْزِيّ (ḵubziyy, “of bread”), nisba of Arabic خُبْز (ḵubz, “bread”), calquing the first element of Artocarpus, Ancient Greek ᾰ̓́ρτος (ắrtos, “bread”).
Singulative noun composed of خَرُّوب (ḵarrūb, “carob”) + ـَة (-a). The coin meaning is a semantic loan from Ancient Greek κερᾱ́τῐον (kerā́tĭon).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χόνδρος (khóndros).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χωρεπίσκοπος (khōrepískopos).

parole.significato: household implement, junk, odds and ends, trinkets
parole.testo: Unknown. Maybe from Ancient Greek δάπις (dápis), via an Aramaic colloquial term which would explain s → š as in قَيْشُور (qayšūr) and إشْقِيل (ʔišqīl), so a doublet of طِنْفَسَة (ṭinfasa).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Δέρβη (Dérbē, “Derbe”), a border town in Lycaonia at the Cilician Gates.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek δάφνη (dáphnē).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥητίνη (rhētínē) in the science translation environment. Doublet of رَجِينَة (rajīna).
Borrowed from Aramaic אֲרוּזָא (ʔăruzzā) / ܐܘܪܘܙܐ (ʔuruzzā), ܪܘܙܐ (rūzā). Doublet of بِرِنْج (birinj).
رِوَاق (riwāq, “portico, stoa”) + ـِيّ (-iyy). Calque of Ancient Greek Στωϊκός (Stōïkós), from στοά (stoá, “stoa”).
From Ancient Greek ζωνάριον (zōnárion), likely via Aramaic זונרא / ܙܘܢܪܐ (zūnārā). See the usage notes for distinctions between various types of belts.

parole.significato: a dish made of yogurt and sour milk mixed with vegetables and boiled and stirred
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζωμός (zōmós).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ζίζυφον (zízuphon). Doublet of زِفْزِف (zifzif) and زُفَيْزَف (zufayzaf, “jujube”). The meaning of oleaster is also encountered in Modern Greek τζιτζιφιά (tzitzifiá).
From Ancient Greek ἰσάτις (isátis, “woad”).
Compare Classical Syriac ܣܪܛܢܐ (sarṭānā), and Hebrew סַרְטָן (sarṭā́n). The medical sense is possibly a semantic loan from Ancient Greek καρκίνος (karkínos).

A corruption of its epithet إِسْكَنْدَرَانِيَّة (ʔiskandarāniyya, literally “Alexandrian”) in the Ancient Greek name of one species δάφνη Ἀλεξάνδρεια (dáphnē Alexándreia), possibly blended with a form of Persian اسپرغم (esparġam, “medicinal herb”), as in Persian Ruscus genus and species are now most
Borrowed from Ancient Greek σκαμμωνία (skammōnía).

Apparently from Ancient Greek σημύδα (sēmúda), a hapax attested in Θεόφραστος often glossed as birch. Perhaps borrowed into Arabic from a manuscript variant or elsewhere with a suffix such as a *σημυδάριον (*sēmudárion) with -άριον (-árion), or this ending is derived from popularity in Arabic, as in

From Ancient Greek σανδαράκινος (sandarákinos, “orange-coloured, sandarac-like”) or another masculine formation from σανδᾰράκη (sandărákē, “sandarac, realgar”), compare خَنْدَرُوس (ḵandarūs) from χόνδρος (khóndros, “spelt; groats; lump, grumous mass”) and دَنْدَرُوس (dandarūs) from δενδροειδής (dend
Borrowed from Ancient Greek σύμφυτον (súmphuton).

Has been identified with Jewish Babylonian Aramaic סַלָּקוּתָא (sallaqūṯā) which occurs in some obscure context in Terumot 8 from which one can only derive that it is a kind of container. Ancient Greek σάλαξ (sálax, “miner’s sieve”) has been suggested for this word. It has also been related to Old A
Borrowed from Ancient Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τοπογραφία (topographía).

parole.significato: tarragon, estragon (Artemisia dracunculus, growing plant and processed form)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek δρακόντιον (drakóntion, “edder-wort, Dracunculus vulgaris”, a plant with similar leaves, confused in pharmacopoeiae as both plants were not everywhere available), from δράκων (drákōn, “dragon, serpent”) relating to the shape of its leaves.

parole.significato: pearl mullet, Alburnus tarichi, a kind of small salted fish from Lake Van
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek τάριχος (tárikhos). Meanwhile in Egypt the same word was obtained from Coptic as بُطَارِخ (buṭāriḵ).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek τέλεσμα (télesma, “payment”).

parole.significato: some Artemisia spp., such as Artemisia inculta and Artemisia judaica and Artemisia vulgaris
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀβρότονον (abrótonon, “Artemisia spp.”). Notwithstanding the word is in Bedouin use.

From the root ع ل ج (ʕ l j) meaning “to be strong or sturdy”, “to be robust or bulky”, “to be massive”, “to be big or thick”, “to be long or tall”; a variant of عَلْجَن (ʕaljan, “a female camel with a bulkier male-like frame; a camel strong enough to use for work”). Probably a calque of Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología).

parole.significato: agarikon, agaric (Laricifomes officinalis, syn. Fomitopsis officinalis and Polyporus officinalis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀγαρικόν (agarikón).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φιλώνειον (philṓneion).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φανός (phanós, “lantern”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek παιωνία (paiōnía).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek φαράσιον (pharásion), other form of πράσιον (prásion), likely connected to the family of derivations connected to πράσινος (prásinos, “green”) like πράσον (práson, “leek”), πράσιος (prásios, “vomit”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek εὐφόρβιον (euphórbion) in the science translation environment.
فَرَس (faras, “horse”) + نَهْر (nahr, “river”). Calque of Ancient Greek ῐ̔πποπότᾰμος (hĭppopótămos).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek ψῆφος (psêphos, “small stone”).

parole.significato: seal (marine animal of the family Phocidae)
parole.testo: Most likely just an international word from Ancient Greek φώκη (phṓkē, “seal”), perhaps with this form in Arabic potentially influenced by فُقْم (fuqm) in the sense of a dog's muzzle. Compare the by-name كَلْبُ البَحْرِ (kalbu l-baḥri, “sea lion, seal”, literally “dog of the sea”) as the Arabs, amon

parole.significato: cork, the bast of the cork oak
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek φελλός (phellós, “cork”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek φολίς (pholís).
Verbal noun of فَلْسَفَ (falsafa, “to philosophize”), either constructed based on فَيْلَسُوف (faylasūf, “philosopher”), or based directly on Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía)

parole.significato: contrivance whereby the feet are held in a bastinado
parole.testo: Ultimately from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx) likely through Aramaic, also with the loaned sense of a “flat-surface, panel, plank, or a wooden surface”; compare Aramaic פּלגּה (plaggā, “drum”) and see Ancient Greek φῠλᾰκή (phŭlăkḗ, “a form of detention, stockade for punishment”).

Belonging to the root ف ل ك (f l k). Perhaps, however, unrelated to etymology 1 and instead from Ancient Greek ἐφόλκιον (ephólkion). Nonetheless, it might be linked to Hebrew פֶּלֶךְ (pélekh, “spindle”), the relationship being "being rounded".

parole.significato: cork, the bast of the cork oak
parole.testo: Not فِلّ (fill, “cork”) + ـِين (-īn, chemical suffix) but, for the age of the word, Ancient Greek φέλλινος (phéllinos, “of cork”).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek πανδοκεῖον (pandokeîon), from πᾰν- (păn-, “all, every”) + δοκ- (dok-, o-grade of the stem of δέχομαι (dékhomai, “to receive”)) + -εῖον (-eîon). The word went through the Arabic phonological shift /p/ to /f/.
From Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos, literally “lover of wisdom”).

parole.significato: skep, scoop, kibble, bucket, dipper (for a well or a mill or for irrigation or an excavator or whatever)
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κάδος (kádos). The form قَدَس (qadas), anciently used in the Ḥijāz and thence exported to Northwestern Arabic, came via Aramaic – Classical Syriac ܩܱܕܣܴܐ (qadsā, qaddəsā).
From Ancient Greek καλόν (kalón) ("beautiful, lovely, good quality, useful, good, right, moral, virtuous, noble").
From Ancient Greek ὠκεανός (ōkeanós). Sense 1 stems from the title of Firuzabadi’s dictionary, the The Encompassing ὠκεανός, which became popular. Doublet of أُوقْيَانُوس (ʔūqyānūs).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κᾰνών (kănṓn). Possibly a doublet of قَنَاة (qanāh).

parole.significato: racially non-Arab Egyptians regardless of religion (such as the Ancient Egyptians or medieval Egyptian converts to Isla…
parole.testo: From Koine Greek Αἰγύπτιος (Aigúptios), from Αἴγυπτος (Aíguptos), from Egyptian ḥwt-kꜣ-ptḥ.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
From Ancient Greek κράνεια (kráneia), κρανία (kranía, “cornel tree”), extensions of κράνον (kránon, “cornel”).

From قَرَشَ (qaraša, “to gnash, to grind (one's teeth)”). Doubtfully from Ancient Greek καρχαρίας (karkharías, “shark”), from κάρχαρος (kárkharos, “sharp, jagged”), also present in Jewish Babylonian Aramaic כרשא (“probably shark”), Latin carcharias, carcharus.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κηρύλος (kērúlos).
From Ancient Greek κραμβίδιον (krambídion), the diminutive of κράμβη (krámbē). Doublet of كُرُنْب (kurunb).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κῐ́στος (kĭ́stos).

parole.significato: costus (both Costus gen. and Saussurea costus (syns. Saussurea lappa, Aucklandia lappa))
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κόστος (kóstos).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).

parole.significato: hedge nettle (Stachys spp., especially the betony (Stachys officinalis))
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek κέστρον (késtron, “betony”) during the science translation movement.
Ultimately from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κισσός (kissós).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κύκνος (kúknos).
From Ancient Greek κάλως (kálōs, “rope, cable”). Aramaic but found as Classical Syriac ܩܠܣܐ at Bar Bahlul.

Derived from Ancient Greek κάλαμος (kálamos). Nöldeke and Jeffery are convinced that it comes thence via Ge'ez ቀለም (ḳäläm, “reed”), while Leslau notes that ቀለም (ḳäläm, “reed”) could come from Arabic. But the meaning “reed” – referring to a plant – is not actually attested for the Arabic word, and gi
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κένταυρος (kéntauros).
From Ancient Greek κενταύρειον (kentaúreion). Doublet of جِنْتَوْرِيَّة (jintawriyya) borrowed from Latin.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κῶλον (kôlon).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek κεράτιον (kerátion, “carat, a Byzantine coin”).
From Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós).

An unclassical word, apparently applying the vulgar tool pattern فَاعُول (fāʕūl) to Ancient Greek χαλινός (khalinós, “bit; thong; part of the tackle of a ship; anything that restrains from the outer”). Also passed into Classical Syriac ܟܠܴܢܳܐ (klānā, “bar or bolt for fastening doors, sera”).

parole.significato: cabbage, kale (various plants of Brassicaceae fam. and their edible foliage)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek κρᾰ́μβη (krắmbē).

parole.significato: washbasin, bucket dipper, bath, a gourd used for ablution
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek χέρνιβον (khérnibon, “washbasin for ritual handwashing”).

parole.significato: the tip of the penis, the glans
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek καμάρᾱ (kamárā) or Latin camara.
Calque of Ancient Greek ἀστὴρ πλανήτης (astḕr planḗtēs, “wandering star, planet”) as distinguished from the fixed stars, from كَوْكَب (kawkab, “star”) + سَيَّار (sayyār, “wanderer”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek χυμείᾱ (khumeíā), from χῠ́μᾰ (khŭ́mă) + -ία (-ía).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek λᾱ́δᾰνον (lā́dănon).
From لَجِئَ (lajiʔa) due to the animal taking refuge in its shell, attested since the 9ᵗʰ century. In the sense of a roll-slide semantic loan from Ancient Greek χελώνη (khelṓnē).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek λῃστής (lēistḗs).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek λείριον (leírion), or one of its Ibero-Romance descendants, living in Spanish lirio and Galician lirio (“lily; iris”).
Relative noun (nisba) composed of مَا هِيَ (mā hiya, “what is it”) + ـِيَّة (-iyya), a calque of Ancient Greek τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι (tò tí ên eînai) used by Aristotle. Compare هُوِيّة (huwiyya).
From Ancient Greek μοχλός (mokhlós, “bar, lever”).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek μυρσίνη (mursínē).

parole.significato: a kind of large container to transport (i.e. on camels) oil or vinegar
parole.testo: Unknown, maybe from a regional derivation of Ancient Greek μάρις (máris, “a liquid measure”) with -ῖνος (-înos), its feminine -ῑ́νη (-ī́nē).
From Ancient Greek μαγνησία (magnēsía) and Μαγνησία (Magnēsía).

Borrowed from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient; malleable material”), related to μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”) and μαλακός (malakós, “soft”). The same term has been acquired via Middle Persian as مَرْهَم (marham).

parole.significato: mulukhiyah (Corchorus gen. et spp., most often Corchorus olitorius, and the vegetable thereof)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek μολόχιον (molókhion, “mallow”) (its plural).

Noun of place from the root ن و ر (n w r) of نُور (nūr, “light, fire”). Cognate with Aramaic מְנָרְתָא (mənārəṯā), Hebrew מְנוֹרָה (mənōrā). Maybe there is a contamination with Ancient Greek μιλιάριον (miliárion, “miles indicator”) as the word means landmark.

Noun of place from the root ن و ر (n w r), relating to "light" and "fire". Cognate with Aramaic מְנָרְתָא (mənārəṯā), Hebrew מְנוֹרָה (mənōrā), Ugaritic 𐎎𐎐𐎗𐎚 (mnrt). Maybe there is a contamination with Ancient Greek μιλιάριον (miliárion, “miles indicator”) if the word means landmark.

From Ancient Greek μαγγανικά (manganiká), probably through Aramaic, found as Jewish Babylonian Aramaic מנגניקון (mangānīqōn) and Classical Syriac ܡܰܢܓܳܢܺܝܩܳܐ (mangānīqā), clearly seen even in Ge'ez መንገኒቃ (mängäniḳa).

Derived from the passive participle of the verb نَشَرَ (našara). In the meaning of prism compare Hebrew מִנְסָרָה (minsará, “prism”) and Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܢܣܝܼܪܵܐ (nsīrā, “prism”). Possibly Calque of Ancient Greek πρίσμα (prísma, “something sawed”).
From نَطَقَ (naṭaqa, “to pronounce, utter”). Etymology 1, noun sense 1 is a calque of Ancient Greek λογῐκός (logĭkós).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek μῆον (mêon).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ).

Derived from the passive participle of وَضَعَ (waḍaʕa, “to put, lay”). The sense “topic, subject” at first in logical discourse as a calque of Ancient Greek ὑποκείμενον (hupokeímenon, literally “that which is laid down, underlying, suggested”).

parole.significato: a kind of metal probe in form of a needle for applying collyrium or other treatments
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek μήλη (mḗlē, “probe”).
نُسْطُور (nusṭūr, “Nestorius”) + ـِيّ (-iyy). The name is from Ancient Greek Νεστόριος (Nestórios).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek νίτρον (nítron).
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ναυπηγός (naupēgós).

From Ancient Greek ναύτης (naútēs, “seaman”) and ναυτίλος (nautílos, “seaman; nautilus mollusc”), possibly via Aramaic, compare the Aramaic borrowings with this ending نُمِّيّ (nummiyy) and سَكِّيّ (sakkiyy) or دُرْدِيّ (durdiyy), though seemingly an old loanword.
Borrowed from Ancient Greek ναῦλος (naûlos).

From the root ه ي ل (h y l) in the sense of a pile or cluster of things together; piled sand, dust particles. A phono-semantic matching of Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “stuff, matter, substance”, literally “wood, raw material”), supported by the presence in Classical Syriac ܗܝܘܠܐ (hiyūlā), ܗܘܠܐ (hūlā),

parole.significato: unformed matter that preceded the existence of the universe
parole.testo: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ὕλη (húlē, “matter”).
Derived from Ancient Greek ὑάκινθος (huákinthos), possibly via Sogdian [script needed] (yγwth /⁠yaγūt⁠/, “ruby”).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἰωνία (Iōnía, “Ionia”).
